unit.unitOverview: Communication means sharing information so that others understand it, by speaking, writing or drawing, and also listening carefully when others share with you. It has two halves that always work together: presenting your ideas clearly, and listening so you really understand what others say back.

explainers.title: Hello, and welcome to your last unit
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This is a special unit, because it is the last one of your Year 4. You have come a long way. This year you have grown all six thinking skills, one at a time, and here they all are together:

This unit is all about that sixth and final skill: Communication. It is a lovely skill to end on, because it is where all your other work finally goes out into the world. You can find things out, think about them, judge them, and work on them with a team. But none of that helps anyone else until you can share it clearly. Communication is how your good thinking reaches other people.

Think about the grown-ups around you. A nurse explaining how to keep a cut clean, a market seller in Mogadishu telling you about her vegetables, a neighbour asking the town to fix a broken well: all of them are communicating, sharing clearly and listening to what others say back. A child who learns this now will be heard, and able to help others, all through their life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful way.
Analysis — looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how good, useful or true something is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas so that others understand you.

explainers.title: So what is communication?
explainers.body:
Lots of people think communication just means talking. It is more than that. Here is a simple meaning you can keep: communication means sharing information so that others understand it, and listening carefully when others share with you. So communication always has two halves that work together.

A good communicator is strong at both halves. If you only talk, you miss what others know. If you only listen, your own good ideas stay stuck inside your head. This unit grows both halves, so you can share an idea and really talk it over with others.
bullets: Presenting — sending your ideas out clearly, by speaking or writing or even drawing a picture, so that others can follow them.
Listening — taking in what other people share, and asking a question when something is not clear.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You might be wondering something clever: how can I learn to present and listen when I study on my own? That is a good question, and the answer is the heart of this unit. You will rehearse with your AI tutor, and then present and listen for real with your group in your teacher sessions. Three kinds of help work together:

So the pattern all through this unit is simple: rehearse with your AI tutor now, then present and listen for real with your group in your next teacher session. In the old way of this subject, a book would say 'present to the class'. In our way, you get ready with your tutor first, as many times as you like, so that when you stand up in front of real people you can do your best. Do not worry if presenting feels a little scary at first. Almost everyone feels that way, and rehearsing in private is exactly how nervous speakers become brave ones.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and do the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. In this unit your tutor has a special job. It is your audience and your rehearsal partner. You can present your idea to it, and it will listen, ask you questions, play the other person, and tell you kindly what was clear and what to make clearer.
Your teacher sessions, about twice a week. This is where you present your best work for real, to a real audience, and listen to what the other learners share. Your group is your real 'class'.

explainers.title: Meet Idris, who is finding his voice
explainers.body:
All year we have followed learners at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. For this last unit, meet Idris. You may remember him from the Collaboration unit: he was the quiet one on Layla's team who was brilliant with numbers, tables and charts. Idris likes to think carefully before he speaks, and standing up in front of people makes his tummy feel funny. So Communication is the skill he most wants to grow, and this unit, it is his turn to lead.

Idris has a problem he really cares about. His class wants to build a wildlife area in a corner of the school grounds, a home for plants and small animals. But they cannot agree. Some want a pond; others worry it is not safe for the little ones. Some want a herb garden or bird boxes; some are not sure they want it at all. Everyone is talking at once, and nobody is really listening. Idris wants to help his class get along and make a fair plan together that everyone is happy with.

And that is the secret at the heart of this unit. The big idea running through it is making peace: helping people who see things differently understand each other and agree. Communication is exactly how you do that. When you share your idea clearly, listen kindly, hear both sides, and ask good questions, you help everyone get along. As you meet each new skill, you will watch how Idris uses it to bring his class together, and you will do the very same thing with an issue you care about.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: sharing what matters, and making peace
explainers.body:
This unit builds one big project we call your Challenge. Your Challenge is to share an issue you care about so clearly, and to listen so kindly, that other people understand it and want to help. You will build a short talk, rehearse it with your AI tutor, and present it for real. Here are three good issues, and any of them could be your Challenge:

Your classmates care about different things. Layla wants more birds to visit the school. Nadia once saw baby turtles hurry to the sea at Berbera and never forgot it. Omar thinks the class is being unfair about the pond. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge. You do not have to choose this very minute. As you meet each skill, keep a note of any issue you would love other people to understand. That feeling, wanting to be heard about something that matters, is the heart of communication.
bullets: A school wildlife area. Should your school make a corner of the grounds into a home for plants and small animals? This is Idris's Challenge, and people have different ideas about it, so it is perfect for making peace.

Protecting wild animals. Should the rare cheetahs that live near the grazing lands be protected, even though they sometimes worry the herders whose goats graze there? This has clear arguments on both sides.

Helping nature near you. Is there a plant or an animal near your home, from the sunbirds in the trees to the sea turtles on the Berbera coast, that you would love other people to care about and protect?

explainers.title: Three steps of communication this year
explainers.body:
Your communication skills will grow in three steps this year, like a young tree. First you are starting the skill, then developing it, then getting better at it. Here is what each step is about:

Do not worry if the first tries feel tricky. Starting is meant to feel like a first try, and each skill below will move you a little further along.
bullets: Starting — being clear and talking about the right thing, and listening so well that you can ask a good question back.
Developing — sharing information in an organised way, hearing both sides of an issue, and planning a talk with a clear beginning, middle and end.
Getting better — being a really good listener, asking relevant questions, and helping a group reach a fair decision together.

explainers.title: Speaking clearly, and about the right thing
explainers.body:
The first skill is to present your idea clearly. To present just means to share information with other people so they understand it. Being clear is one part of this. The other part is being relevant. Relevant means talking about the right thing, the thing that matters, instead of wandering off to something else. A clear, relevant speaker is easy to follow.

Before you speak, it helps to think about four small things. We call this the When I speak plan:
bullets: Message — what is my main idea? How can I say it as clearly as possible?
Audience — who am I speaking to? What do they need to know?
Purpose — why am I speaking? To tell them something, or to persuade them?
Structure — what order should I use, from start to finish?

explainers.title: Listening, and reading how people feel
explainers.body:
The second half of communication is listening, and it is a real skill. You pay full attention, you follow what the person says, and when they finish you respond, often by asking a question about what they said. A good question shows you were really listening.

When people talk about an idea, you can often work out how they feel about it, just from the clues in their words. Some sound happy about it. Some sound not sure. Some sound unhappy. Listening for these clues helps you understand everyone, not just the loudest voice.

explainers.title: Giving reasons, to persuade
explainers.body:
Sometimes you want to persuade people, which means helping others agree with your idea or want to join in. You do not persuade by talking louder. You persuade by giving good reasons, one after another, in a tidy order. Little joining words, called connectives, help you line up your reasons so they are easy to follow.

Here are useful connectives for a persuasive case:
bullets: Firstly, ... for your first reason.
Secondly, ... for your next reason.
This is because ... to explain a reason.
In addition, ... and Furthermore, ... to add more reasons.
Finally, it is clear that ... to finish strongly.

explainers.title: Hearing both sides of an issue
explainers.body:
Many issues have two sides, with reasons for and reasons against. A strong communicator does not just shout for their own side. They listen carefully to both sides, asking questions and taking notes, so they really understand the whole issue.

Near Hargeisa, some rare cheetahs live on the grazing lands, where herding families keep their goats. There is a real disagreement about them. Here are two people, each explaining their side in a tidy way.

explainers.title: Planning a talk with a skeleton plan
explainers.body:
When you present a case, a plan stops your talk from wandering. We use a skeleton plan: a simple frame that holds your talk up, like the bones that hold up a body. A good skeleton plan for a persuasive talk has four parts, in this order:

The clever part is that you do not hide the other side. You include the arguments against fairly, in the middle. This makes your talk feel fair, and, oddly, it makes people trust you more, because they can see you have thought about both sides.
bullets: Introduction — say what the issue is, and what you think.
Arguments for — your reasons to support the idea.
Arguments against — the other side's reasons, said fairly.
Conclusion — sum up, and say what you want to happen.

explainers.title: Being a really good listener
explainers.body:
The last two skills come back to listening, because a great communicator is a great listener. Being a really good listener is called active listening: listening on purpose, and showing the speaker you are paying attention. Here are the things good listeners do:

Which of these matters most? People do not always agree, and that is fine. Some say letting the speaker finish matters most; some say asking a question shows you truly listened. There is no single right answer. What matters is that a good listener makes the speaker feel heard.
bullets: Make eye contact with the speaker.
Keep still and quiet while they talk.
Smile or nod to show you are paying attention.
Let the speaker finish before you speak.
Say small things like I see or I understand.
When they finish, ask a question or add an idea of your own.

explainers.title: Asking good questions, and deciding together
explainers.body:
When you listen to lots of people, you help most by asking relevant questions: questions that are truly about what was said, and that help everyone understand better. Then a group can put all its ideas together and reach a shared decision: one choice the whole group agrees on, after everyone shares clearly, listens, and weighs it up fairly.

Idris's class wants to give a little money to a charity that helps wildlife and nature. A charity is a group that helps others. Three learners each found out about a different one. Their job is to share, listen, ask questions, and decide together.

explainers.title: How communication uses your other five skills
explainers.body:
Communication is the last skill for a good reason. It gathers up every skill you have grown this year and sends them all out into the world. Look how each one lives inside a good talk:

So communication is not a brand-new skill on its own. It is the moment all six skills work together, because every hour you spent this year finding out, thinking, judging, reflecting and working with others is the strong thinking behind a message worth hearing.
bullets: Research gives you the facts you share, so your idea is true and not just a guess.
Analysis gives you the reasons, and the two sides, that make up your case.
Evaluation helps you choose your strongest, most relevant points, and leave out the weak ones.
Reflection helps you notice how your own view has changed, so you can answer why do you think that?
Collaboration taught you to listen to others and value their ideas, which is the whole listening half of communication.

explainers.title: Putting it all together
explainers.body: You have now met every communication skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into simple steps you can use to share any idea:
bullets: Think about your message, audience, purpose and structure before you speak.
Be clear and relevant, and give reasons with connectives to persuade.
Listen for how people feel, and respond with a friendly question.
Hear both sides fairly, asking questions and taking notes.
Plan your talk with a skeleton plan: introduction, for, against, conclusion.
Be an active listener, and ask relevant questions.
Help your group reach a shared decision, and explain it with reasons.

explainers.title: Well done: you have finished your Year 4 skills journey
explainers.body:
Take a moment to see how far you have come. You began by learning to research the world carefully. You learned to analyse an issue and ask why things happen, to evaluate how good and true different ideas are, to reflect honestly on your own learning, and to collaborate kindly with a team. And now, with communication, you have learned to share all of that clearly, and to listen well, so that you can be heard.

These six skills are yours to keep. They are not just for Global Perspectives, or even just for school. They are the skills of a thoughtful, fair and helpful person: someone who finds things out, thinks them through, works well with others, and speaks up for what matters.

Well done for finishing your Year 4 journey at Ehel Academy. Be proud of the thinker you have become. Next year you will grow these same six skills even further. The world needs young people who can find out the truth, think clearly, work together, and communicate with honesty and kindness. This year, you have started to become exactly that.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
In this unit we will use real topics, such as a school wildlife garden, wild cheetahs, and helping nature.
But the real prize is not the topic. It is to become a clear, kind communicator who can share almost any idea, and listen well to almost anyone.

bigIdeas.title: The two halves of communication
lines: Presenting: How can I share my idea so that others understand it clearly?
Listening: When someone else shares, what question can I ask to understand them better?
A strong communicator keeps swapping between these two halves, like a good game of catch.

bigIdeas.title: Caring for others and for nature
lines: Helping people and looking after the living world is something families all over the world care about.
Giving to help others is called sadaqah in Islam, and it is also taught as charity in Christianity. Both encourage kindness to people and care for creation.
Whatever your family believes, everyone can help look after nature. Choosing to give, and deciding together how, is a kind and grown-up thing to do.
A relevant question, like What matters most here? or What is good about choosing the one closest to home?, can help a whole group find its way to a fair, shared choice.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Choose one issue you would love other people to understand, such as a school wildlife area, protecting a wild animal, or helping nature near you.
You will build a short talk about it, step by step, and present it at the end.
Pick something you really care about, because it is much easier to speak well about what matters to you.

bigIdeas.title: What the learners say about the pond
lines: Grace: A pond would be wonderful, it will bring frogs and dragonflies to our school.
Malik: I am not sure a pond is safe for the very little children.
Talia: The plus points are much bigger than the worries, I think we should do it.
Zane: I have decided it would be a step backwards, and I do not want one.

bigIdeas.title: Connectives to line up your reasons
lines: Firstly, ... Secondly, ...
This is because ...
In addition, ... Furthermore, ...
Finally, it is clear that ...

bigIdeas.title: Source: Should we protect the cheetahs?
lines: Near Hargeisa, in the Horn of Africa, some rare cheetahs live on the grazing lands. There are very few of them left in the world.
A herder is worried. The cheetahs frighten the goats, and when the goats scatter, some get lost or hurt. Herding is already a hard way to make a living, and losing goats makes it harder.

A ranger from the wildlife centre sees it differently. Cheetahs are rare and have lived here a long time. Rangers watch and count them. Cheetahs mostly hunt wild gazelle, not goats, and a strong thorn pen keeps the goats safe at night.

bigIdeas.title: What good listeners do
lines: Make eye contact, and keep still and quiet.
Smile or nod to show you are listening.
Let the speaker finish before you speak.
Say I see or I understand, then ask a question or add an idea.

bigIdeas.title: Three charities to choose between
lines: A group that protects sea-turtle nesting beaches on the Berbera coast.
The wildlife centre near Hargeisa that cares for rescued cheetahs.
A group that plants trees, giving birds and bees a home.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 6 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Communication. This is my last unit of Year 4.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, why is it not enough to find out about something, if I cannot share it clearly?
Then tell your tutor whether you find presenting or listening harder, and why. Ask it to be your audience and rehearsal partner for this whole unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one small thing you know a lot about, like a game, a place, or an animal.
Share it in three clear sentences: what it is, one important fact, and why it matters.
Ask the tutor: did you understand my main idea, and did I stay on the right thing, or did I wander off?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to say three short sentences about an idea, one happy, one not sure, and one unhappy.
Listen, and tell the tutor how each speaker feels, and which words gave you the clue.
Then practise responding kindly: ask one of the speakers a friendly question about what they said.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor an idea you would like to persuade people about.
Give three reasons, using the connectives Firstly, Secondly, and In addition.
Ask the tutor: were my reasons clear and in a good order, and which reason was the strongest?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to sit in the hot seat and answer as the herder, while you ask two questions.
Then ask it to answer as Ms Silva the ranger, and ask her two questions too.
Take notes, then tell the tutor what each person is most worried about, and what each one wants.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue and what you think about it.
Ask it to help you fill in a skeleton plan: introduction, arguments for, arguments against, conclusion.
Then ask: does my order flow well, and did I say the arguments against fairly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to tell you about an idea for a whole minute, without stopping.
Listen actively: notice when you want to butt in, and wait instead. Jot one or two quick notes.
When it finishes, say I see, then ask one question about what it said. Ask the tutor if you were a good listener.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about two good causes you could give to. Ask it to help you think of questions to compare them.
Practise asking: Which is closest to us? and Would one big gift help more than several small ones?
Then make your own choice, and tell the tutor your decision with two clear reasons for it.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, your message, your audience, and your purpose.
Ask it: is my issue a good size to share in a few minutes, or is it too big?
Ask the tutor to help you say your main message in one clear, simple sentence.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your sorting and your clues to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you read each person's feeling correctly.
Then ask the tutor to say a new sentence about the pond, and you tell it how that speaker feels.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your persuasive reasons to your AI tutor.
Ask it: were my reasons clear, in a good order, and easy to follow?
Ask the tutor which reason was the strongest, and which one I could make stronger.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to sit in the hot seat as the herder, and ask it your question.
Then ask it to answer as the ranger, and ask it your second question.
Take notes, then tell the tutor what each person most wants, and which side surprised you.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four-part skeleton plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your order flows well, and whether you said the arguments against fairly.
Ask the tutor to check that your conclusion ends with one clear thing you want to happen.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole talk to your AI tutor from start to finish.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and a wish: two things that worked, and one thing to improve.
Ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you, so you can check your main message came through.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After your listening practice, ask your AI tutor whether you were a good listener.
Ask it: was my question relevant, meaning was it really about what I said?
Ask the tutor to suggest one even better question you could have asked.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your three charities and your questions for comparing them.
Ask it to play a classmate who prefers a different charity, so you can practise listening and asking questions.
Then tell the tutor your final choice, with two clear reasons.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three checkpoint sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from how my talk went, what is one communication skill I should keep practising?
Ask the tutor to help you plan how you could share this same idea with a bigger audience one day.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrites now show good listening and stay on the right thing.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to reword any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more story like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your whole-year reflection to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how much you have grown across all six skills since the start of the year.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill to carry forward and keep sharpening, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A family touch
lines: Ask someone at home about a time two people they know did not agree, and how they sorted it out.
Ask them: what helps most when people see things differently? Listening? Being kind? Explaining clearly?
Bring their answer to your next teacher session. The grown-ups around you know a lot about making peace.

speakingPrompts.title: Idris shares his part of the plan clearly
lines: Idris's class has drawn a map of the wildlife area, split into zones. Each child found out about a different zone.

Idris found out about the bird-box zone. When it is his turn, he says it clearly: In the bird-box zone we will put up five wooden boxes in the acacia trees, so small birds like sunbirds have a safe place to nest.
He does not wander off to talk about lunch or football. He stays relevant, and tells only what matters.
Then he listens as the others share their zones, and together the class labels the whole map.
Clear presenting is not about big words or a loud voice. It is about knowing your one main idea and helping the other person follow you step by step.

speakingPrompts.title: Idris listens for how his class feels
lines: Grace says: I love the pond idea, it will bring frogs and dragonflies. She sounds happy about it. (A positive clue.)
Malik says: I am not sure a pond is safe for the little ones. He sounds unsure. (A not-sure clue.)
Zane says: I really do not think we should have a pond at all. He sounds unhappy. (A negative clue.)
Idris listens carefully and works out how each person feels. Then, instead of arguing, he asks Malik a gentle question: What would make the pond feel safe to you?

When you listen, you do not have to agree with everything; you are just trying to understand. And when you want to tell someone you agree or disagree, you can do it kindly: I agree, and I would add ... or I see it a little differently, because ... Kind words keep everyone friendly, even when they do not think the same.

speakingPrompts.title: Idris persuades the class to make the grounds greener
lines: Idris wants to persuade his class to make the school grounds a better place for plants and animals. He lines up his reasons.
Firstly, we could plant a herb garden, so the kitchen has fresh herbs. Secondly, we could put up bird boxes. This is because birds help us by eating insects.
In addition, we could count the different species we see, to learn what lives here. Furthermore, a few frankincense and aloe plants would suit our dry weather.
Finally, it is clear that a wildlife area would make our school greener, and a happier place for everyone.
See how the connectives turn a jumble of ideas into a clear, strong case?

speakingPrompts.title: Two organised opinions about the cheetahs
lines: Amara's uncle, a herder, is worried: Firstly, the cheetahs frighten our goats. Secondly, when the goats are frightened they scatter, and some get lost or hurt. Thirdly, herding is already a hard way to make a living. In conclusion, I am worried about my family's animals.

Ms Silva, a ranger from the wildlife centre, sees it differently: Firstly, cheetahs are rare, and they have lived on this land for a very long time. Secondly, our rangers watch and count them, so we know how they are doing. Thirdly, cheetahs mostly hunt wild gazelle, not goats, and a strong thorn pen keeps the goats safe at night. In conclusion, we can protect the cheetahs and the goats at the same time.

To understand each person better, you can write questions to ask them, and try hot-seating: someone sits in the 'hot seat' and answers as if they were that person. As you listen, you take notes and finish sentences like: The herder is worried because ... He wants ... The ranger thinks ... She wants ... By the end, you understand both sides, even the one you did not expect.

speakingPrompts.title: Idris plans a talk about a class nature walk
lines: Introduction: We have a choice about our next trip, and I think a nature walk to see the birds and plants would be a wonderful idea.
Arguments for: It would be fun. We would learn about the plants and animals near us. It is good exercise, and we would remember the creatures we saw.
Arguments against: Some worry there is not enough time, and that assessment week is coming soon.
Conclusion: We would learn in so many ways on a nature walk, so I hope our class will choose it.

You can use the very same shape to plan your own talk, such as Idris's case for making the school grounds better for plants and animals. Fill in each part, and your jumble of ideas becomes a clear path your audience can follow.

speakingPrompts.title: Idris shows he is really listening
lines: Omar presents his idea that the class should grow vegetables next to the herb garden.
Idris makes eye contact, keeps still, and nods now and then. He does not butt in, even when he has an idea.
When Omar finishes, Idris says: I see, that is interesting. Then he asks: Which vegetables would grow well in our dry weather?
Omar feels really listened to, and answers happily. Good listening made him want to share even more.

speakingPrompts.title: The class decides which charity to help
lines: Idris found out about a group that protects sea-turtle nesting beaches on the Berbera coast.
Layla found out about the wildlife centre near Hargeisa that cares for rescued cheetahs.
Omar found out about a group that plants trees, which gives birds and bees a home.

Each one shares clearly. The others listen and ask questions: Which one is closest to us? Would one big gift help more than lots of small ones? Then the class votes and decides together, and Idris explains their choice with reasons.

speakingPrompts.title: Idris's whole journey, from a noisy class to a fair plan
lines: He shared his part of the wildlife map clearly, and listened for how everyone felt about the pond.
He gave tidy reasons with connectives, and heard both sides of the cheetah issue with questions and notes.
He planned a talk with a skeleton plan, listened actively, and asked good questions.
So the quiet boy who was good with numbers found his voice, and helped his class reach a fair decision and make peace.
In the Activities file, you will do these very same steps, building and sharing your own idea, with your AI tutor rehearsing beside you the whole way.

speakingPrompts.title: A model, to show the shape
lines: Firstly, we could plant a herb garden, so we have fresh herbs for the kitchen.
Secondly, we could put up bird boxes, in addition to a shady corner of acacia trees.
Finally, it is clear that a greener school would be a happier place for everyone.

speakingPrompts.title: A model skeleton plan you can copy the shape of
lines: Introduction: I think our school should make a wildlife area, because it would help plants and animals.
Arguments for: It would bring birds and butterflies. It would be a calm, green place to learn.
Arguments against: Some worry a pond might not be safe for little children.
Conclusion: We could have the garden without a deep pond, so let us start our wildlife area this term.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring a short, clear idea you have rehearsed, about the wildlife area or another issue.
Present it to your group, then listen carefully as others present theirs, and ask each person one friendly question.
This is real communication: you rehearsed with your AI tutor, and now you present and listen for real.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Bring your skeleton plan and give your short talk to your group.
Then listen to another learner's talk, and see if you can spot their introduction, their reasons, and their conclusion.
Tell them one thing that was clear, and ask them one question about their idea.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Share the charity you found out about, and listen carefully as others share theirs.
As a group, ask questions and reach one shared decision that everyone can accept.
Notice how listening well and asking good questions helped your group make peace and agree.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Try hot-seating as a group: one person answers as the herder, another as the ranger.
Everyone else listens, takes notes, and asks one relevant question.
Afterwards, share what each side is most worried about, and see if the group can think of a fair answer for both.

teacherSessions.title: Present it for real
lines: Bring your talk to your next teacher session and present it to your group.
Afterwards, present it to your family or a neighbour, and ask them what they understood.
Write down one thing that went well, and one thing you will do even better next time.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Listen carefully to another learner's idea, showing that you are paying attention.
When they finish, ask them one relevant, kind question about what they said.

teacherSessions.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Each person shares the charity they found out about, clearly and briefly.
The group listens, asks questions, and reaches one shared decision everyone can accept.
Choose one person to report the decision, with the reasons behind it.

starting: be clear and relevant when I talk about an issue
listen to what someone tells me in a discussion, and respond by asking them a question
developing: present information about an issue in an organised way
listen to what others say in discussions, and respond by asking questions and sharing my own ideas
gettingBetter: present information about an issue in a clear and organised way
join in discussions by listening, asking relevant questions and sharing my own ideas

toolkit.title: The communication steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your idea, good communication follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel stuck.
items: Plan what to say: think about your message, audience, purpose and structure.
Be clear and relevant: stay on the right thing, and give reasons to persuade.
Listen well: read how people feel, and respond with a friendly question.
Hear both sides: ask questions and take notes to understand for and against.
Plan your talk: use a skeleton plan of introduction, for, against, conclusion.
Be an active listener: and ask relevant questions.
Decide together: help your group reach a fair, shared decision.

toolkit.title: What is communication?
toolkit.intro:
Communication means sharing information so that others understand it, by speaking, writing or drawing, and also listening carefully when others share with you. It has two halves that always work together: presenting your ideas clearly, and listening so you really understand what others say back.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, be clear: know your main idea, stay on the right thing, and put your reasons in a good order. Second, be kind and fair: listen to other people, hear both sides, and ask friendly questions. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: The two halves of communication
toolkit.intro: Communication is always two things at once. A strong communicator keeps swapping between them, like a good game of catch. Keep both in mind whenever you plan a talk or take part in a discussion.

rows: Sending your ideas out clearly, by speaking or writing.
Say your main idea, then give one point at a time, in a good order.
Taking in what others share, and asking about anything unclear.
Pay full attention, notice the key points, then ask a friendly question.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 4 Communication learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your communication skills grow in three steps this year. Here are the real learning goals for each step, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: The When I speak plan
toolkit.intro: Before you present, think about these four things. They help you get ready to speak clearly.

headers: When I speak, I think about ...
rows: What is my main idea? How can I say it as clearly as possible?
Who am I speaking to? What do they need to know?
Why am I speaking? To tell them something, to persuade them, or to argue for or against?
How should I order it? What is the best order, from start to finish?

toolkit.title: The skeleton plan for a persuasive talk
toolkit.intro: Copy this frame to plan any talk where you want to persuade. Fill each part with your own idea. The clever bit is putting the other side, the arguments against, in the middle, said fairly.

rows: Say what the issue is, and what I think about it.
My reasons to support the idea.
The other side's reasons, said fairly.
Sum up, and say the one thing I want to happen.

toolkit.title: Connectives to persuade
toolkit.intro: Use these little joining words to line up your reasons, so your case is easy to follow.
items: Firstly, ... for your first reason.
Secondly, ... for your next reason.
This is because ... to explain a reason.
In addition, ... to add another reason.
Furthermore, ... to add one more.
Finally, it is clear that ... to finish strongly.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for asking questions
toolkit.intro: When someone finishes sharing, respond with a relevant question. These help you understand their idea better.
items: Could you tell me more about ...?
What do you mean by ...?
Why do you think ...?
How do you know that?
Can you explain ... again, please?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for sharing ideas and being kind
toolkit.intro: Use these to share your own idea, and to agree or disagree kindly, so everyone stays friendly.
items: I think ... because ...
My idea is ...
I agree with you, and I would add ...
I see it a little differently, because ...
That is a good point. What about ...?

toolkit.title: Presenting with confidence
toolkit.intro:
When you present for real, in your teacher session or at home, how you speak matters as much as what you say. These simple habits help your audience listen.

You will not get all of these right at once, and that is fine. Pick just one to focus on each time you rehearse, and it will slowly become a habit.
items: Slow down. Speak a little more slowly than feels natural, so every word is clear.
Look up. Glance at your audience, not only at your page.
Breathe. A slow breath before you start steadies a nervous voice.
Stand tall. Calm hands and a steady stance help people focus on your words.

toolkit.title: Two stars and a wish
toolkit.intro: When your AI tutor, your teacher or a family member gives you feedback, ask for it in a kind, useful shape: two stars and a wish. The two stars are two things that worked well. The wish is the one thing that would make it even better. Give feedback to others the same way. It keeps everyone brave enough to keep trying, and it always leaves the speaker with one clear thing to improve next time.

checklists.title: Checklist: Am I a good listener?
checklists.intro: Being a really good listener is called active listening. Tick each one, and you will show any speaker that you are truly paying attention.
items: I make eye contact with the speaker.
I keep still and quiet while they talk.
I smile or nod to show I am paying attention.
I let the speaker finish before I speak.
I say small things like I see or I understand.
When they finish, I ask a question or add an idea of my own.

challenge.intro:
You have now built and shared a real piece of communication. Pull it together by finishing these three sentences about your Challenge, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. You will look back at it during Reflection, where you will think not just about this unit, but about your whole year of six skills.
checkpoints: The message I most wanted people to understand was ...
When I presented it, I was proud that ...
One thing I would do differently next time is ...

activities.title: Choose your issue and plan what to say
activities.label: Activity 1: Choose your issue and plan what to say
activities.intro: Every talk starts with a clear idea. First choose your issue, then use the When I speak plan to get ready: message, audience, purpose, and structure.
steps: Write your issue in one sentence: 'The issue I want to share is ...'.
Write your message (your main idea), your audience (who you will speak to), and your purpose (to tell them, or to persuade them?).
Write one sentence saying what you think about the issue, so your audience always knows where you stand.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, your message, your audience, and your purpose.
Ask it: is my issue a good size to share in a few minutes, or is it too big?
Ask the tutor to help you say your main message in one clear, simple sentence.

activities.title: Listen, and read how people feel
activities.label: Activity 2: Listen, and read how people feel
activities.intro: A good communicator can tell how people feel about an idea, just from their words. Read what these four learners say about building a school pond. Sort each one into happy, not sure, or unhappy, and write the clue that helped you.
steps: Sort each speaker into happy, not sure, or unhappy about the pond.
For each one, write the word or phrase that gave you the clue.
Choose one speaker and write a friendly question you could ask them about what they said.

boxes.title: What the learners say about the pond
lines: Grace: A pond would be wonderful, it will bring frogs and dragonflies to our school.
Malik: I am not sure a pond is safe for the very little children.
Talia: The plus points are much bigger than the worries, I think we should do it.
Zane: I have decided it would be a step backwards, and I do not want one.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your sorting and your clues to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you read each person's feeling correctly.
Then ask the tutor to say a new sentence about the pond, and you tell it how that speaker feels.

activities.title: Give reasons to persuade
activities.label: Activity 3: Give reasons to persuade
activities.intro: Now practise persuading with tidy reasons. Think of an idea to make somewhere better for plants and animals, such as your school grounds or a place near your home. Use connectives to line up your reasons.
steps: Write your idea in one sentence, such as: We should make our school grounds better for plants and animals.
Write at least three reasons, each starting with a connective from the box above.
Finish with a strong sentence starting: Finally, it is clear that ...

boxes.title: Connectives to line up your reasons
lines: Firstly, ... Secondly, ...
This is because ...
In addition, ... Furthermore, ...
Finally, it is clear that ...

boxes.title: A model, to show the shape
lines: Firstly, we could plant a herb garden, so we have fresh herbs for the kitchen.
Secondly, we could put up bird boxes, in addition to a shady corner of acacia trees.
Finally, it is clear that a greener school would be a happier place for everyone.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your persuasive reasons to your AI tutor.
Ask it: were my reasons clear, in a good order, and easy to follow?
Ask the tutor which reason was the strongest, and which one I could make stronger.

activities.title: Hear both sides, and ask questions
activities.label: Activity 4: Hear both sides, and ask questions
activities.intro: A fair communicator listens to both sides. Read the short source below about the wild cheetahs that live near the grazing lands, where herding families keep their goats. Your job is to understand both sides.
steps: Write down two things the herder is worried about.
Write down two reasons the ranger gives for protecting the cheetahs.
Write two questions, one you would like to ask the herder, and one for the ranger.

boxes.title: Source: Should we protect the cheetahs?
lines: Near Hargeisa, in the Horn of Africa, some rare cheetahs live on the grazing lands. There are very few of them left in the world.
A herder is worried. The cheetahs frighten the goats, and when the goats scatter, some get lost or hurt. Herding is already a hard way to make a living, and losing goats makes it harder.

A ranger from the wildlife centre sees it differently. Cheetahs are rare and have lived here a long time. Rangers watch and count them. Cheetahs mostly hunt wild gazelle, not goats, and a strong thorn pen keeps the goats safe at night.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to sit in the hot seat as the herder, and ask it your question.
Then ask it to answer as the ranger, and ask it your second question.
Take notes, then tell the tutor what each person most wants, and which side surprised you.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Try hot-seating as a group: one person answers as the herder, another as the ranger.
Everyone else listens, takes notes, and asks one relevant question.
Afterwards, share what each side is most worried about, and see if the group can think of a fair answer for both.

activities.title: Build your skeleton plan
activities.label: Activity 5: Build your skeleton plan
activities.intro: Now give your talk its bones. A skeleton plan sets the order of your ideas, so your audience can follow you. Use the four-part shape from the Lesson file.
steps: Introduction: write one line naming your issue and what you think.
Arguments for: write two reasons that support your idea.
Arguments against: write one reason from the other side, said fairly.
Conclusion: sum up, and write the one thing you want to happen.

boxes.title: A model skeleton plan you can copy the shape of
lines: Introduction: I think our school should make a wildlife area, because it would help plants and animals.
Arguments for: It would bring birds and butterflies. It would be a calm, green place to learn.
Arguments against: Some worry a pond might not be safe for little children.
Conclusion: We could have the garden without a deep pond, so let us start our wildlife area this term.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four-part skeleton plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your order flows well, and whether you said the arguments against fairly.
Ask the tutor to check that your conclusion ends with one clear thing you want to happen.

activities.title: Rehearse your talk, then present it for real
activities.label: Activity 6: Rehearse your talk, then present it for real
activities.intro:
This is the big one. Put your introduction, reasons and conclusion together into one short talk, then rehearse it fully before you present it. Rehearsing with your AI tutor is exactly how nerves shrink and clear speaking grows.

As you rehearse, practise the way you speak, not just the words. Speak a little more slowly than feels natural, so every word is clear. Look up at your audience, not only at your page. And take a slow breath before you begin, because calm breathing steadies a nervous voice.
steps: Put your whole talk in order, following your skeleton plan.
Read it aloud once on your own, slowly and clearly.
Rehearse it with your AI tutor as your audience, at least twice, making it a little better each time.
Then present it for real in your teacher session, and if you can, to your family at home.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole talk to your AI tutor from start to finish.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and a wish: two things that worked, and one thing to improve.
Ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you, so you can check your main message came through.

boxes.title: Present it for real
lines: Bring your talk to your next teacher session and present it to your group.
Afterwards, present it to your family or a neighbour, and ask them what they understood.
Write down one thing that went well, and one thing you will do even better next time.

activities.title: Practise active listening
activities.label: Activity 7: Practise active listening
activities.intro: Communication is two-way, so this activity grows your listening. You will practise active listening: showing a speaker that you are really paying attention, and asking a good question at the end.
steps: Ask your AI tutor to tell you about an idea for a whole minute.
As it speaks, jot one or two quick notes, and notice when you want to butt in, but wait.
When it finishes, say I see, then ask one relevant question about what it said.

boxes.title: What good listeners do
lines: Make eye contact, and keep still and quiet.
Smile or nod to show you are listening.
Let the speaker finish before you speak.
Say I see or I understand, then ask a question or add an idea.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After your listening practice, ask your AI tutor whether you were a good listener.
Ask it: was my question relevant, meaning was it really about what I said?
Ask the tutor to suggest one even better question you could have asked.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Listen carefully to another learner's idea, showing that you are paying attention.
When they finish, ask them one relevant, kind question about what they said.

activities.title: Reach a shared decision
activities.label: Activity 8: Reach a shared decision
activities.intro:
For your last activity, you will help a group reach a shared decision: one choice everyone agrees on. Your class wants to give a little money to a charity that helps wildlife and nature. Three learners each found out about a different one.

There is no single right answer. Helping others and caring for the living world is something families all over the world value. Whatever your family believes, everyone can help look after nature, and deciding together how to help is a kind and grown-up thing to do.
steps: For each charity, write one good reason to choose it.
Write two questions that would help a group decide, such as: Which one is closest to us?
Make your own choice, and write two reasons for your decision.

boxes.title: Three charities to choose between
lines: A group that protects sea-turtle nesting beaches on the Berbera coast.
The wildlife centre near Hargeisa that cares for rescued cheetahs.
A group that plants trees, giving birds and bees a home.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your three charities and your questions for comparing them.
Ask it to play a classmate who prefers a different charity, so you can practise listening and asking questions.
Then tell the tutor your final choice, with two clear reasons.

boxes.title: In your next teacher session
lines: Each person shares the charity they found out about, clearly and briefly.
The group listens, asks questions, and reaches one shared decision everyone can accept.
Choose one person to report the decision, with the reasons behind it.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 12 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does communication mean?
practice.answer: Communication means sharing information so others understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening carefully when others share with you. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Communication has two halves: presenting, and ______.
practice.answer: Listening.

practice.prompt: Name two ways you can present information to others.
practice.answer: Any two of: speaking, writing, drawing a picture.

practice.prompt: What does it mean to be relevant when you talk about an issue?
practice.answer: Relevant means talking about the right thing, the thing that matters, instead of wandering off to something else.

practice.prompt: In the When I speak plan, name the four things to think about (one starts with M, one A, one P, one S).
practice.answer: Message, Audience, Purpose, Structure.

practice.prompt: Name two connectives you could use to line up your reasons when you persuade.
practice.answer: Any two of: Firstly, Secondly, This is because, In addition, Furthermore, Finally.

practice.prompt: Put the four parts of a skeleton plan in order: conclusion, arguments for, introduction, arguments against.
practice.answer: Introduction, arguments for, arguments against, conclusion.

practice.prompt: Why does a fair talk include the arguments against your own idea?
practice.answer: Because saying the other side fairly, and answering it, makes your talk feel fair, and helps people trust you more, since you have thought about both sides.

practice.prompt: Name two things a good active listener does.
practice.answer: Any two of: make eye contact, keep still and quiet, smile or nod, let the speaker finish, say I see or I understand, ask a question at the end.

practice.prompt: Write one relevant question you could ask a speaker after they finish.
practice.answer: Any relevant question about what the speaker said, such as: What do you mean by that? or Why do you think that?

practice.prompt: A choice that a whole group agrees on together is called a shared ______.
practice.answer: Decision (a shared decision).

practice.prompt: Name two of the six Global Perspectives skills that communication uses.
practice.answer: Any two of: Research, Analysis, Evaluation, Reflection, Collaboration.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each communication word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Presenting
options: A. The people you are speaking to.
B. Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.
C. To help others agree with your idea or want to join in.
D. Listening with your whole attention, and showing the speaker you are listening.
E. Truly about the right thing, the thing that matters.
F. A simple frame that sets the order of your talk: introduction, for, against, conclusion.
practice.answer: B — Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Relevant
practice.answer: E — Truly about the right thing, the thing that matters.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Persuade
practice.answer: C — To help others agree with your idea or want to join in.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Audience
practice.answer: A — The people you are speaking to.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Skeleton plan
practice.answer: F — A simple frame that sets the order of your talk: introduction, for, against, conclusion.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Active listening
practice.answer: D — Listening with your whole attention, and showing the speaker you are listening.

practice.intro: These short stories ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Nadia wants to persuade her class to plant a herb garden. What connectives could she use to line up her reasons?
practice.answer: She could use connectives like Firstly, Secondly, In addition, and Finally, to line up her reasons in a clear order.

practice.prompt: Malik only ever talks about his own side of an issue. What is he missing, and what should he do to be fair?
practice.answer: He is missing the other side. He should fairly say one argument against his own idea, and then answer it, which makes his talk fairer and stronger.

practice.prompt: Grace finishes her talk without saying what she wants to happen. Which part of her talk is weak, and what should she add?
practice.answer: Her conclusion is weak, because she never says what she wants to happen. She should add one clear thing she wants, such as: so let us start our garden this term.

practice.prompt: While Karim listens to a classmate, he is not sure how their idea would work. What relevant question could he ask?
practice.answer: He should ask a relevant question, such as: How would your idea work, or What do you mean by that?

practice.prompt: Idris's group cannot agree which charity to help. How could they reach a fair, shared decision together?
practice.answer: They could each share their charity clearly, listen to the others, ask questions like which is closest to us, then vote or find a middle way and agree together.

mistakes: Diving in without saying what your main idea is.
Wandering off to something that is not relevant.
Talking so much that you never listen or ask a question.
Only ever talking about your own side of an issue.
Butting in before the speaker has finished.
Forgetting to end with one clear thing you want to happen.
